As yet unknown and unforeseen enemies would be a rational answer , but not if Trump wants to make friends with them all . <p> ' Like Trump 's infamously unfinished and useless wall along the Mexican border , his Golden Dome is supposedly " visionary " , but is , in reality , flawed and vastly expensive ' ( AP ) <p> If that fails , then the Golden Dome system might be useful , but there 's nothing in principle preventing the Chinese from developing their own Dome -- they have the money and probably the technology -- and exporting it to their allies in Moscow , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ balance of arms , no one can say . <p> As the Israeli Iron Dome also proves , such innovation can create unintended consequences . Because the Iron Dome works so well , it has restrained Iranian aggression and sponsorship of Houthi and other Tehran-sponsored terrorism . That 's a good thing . But it has also liberated Israel from any restraints in waging its own wars . <p> The deterrent effect on Israeli policy of the missile arsenal owned by Iran and its allies , such as Hezbollah , has been neutralised , and all hell has now broken loose . Israel may in one sense be safer thanks to Iron Dome , but the consequent destabilisation of the region has not added to its long-term security . It might well make Iran even more determined to acquire a nuclear weapon -- plus a Dome of its own . <p> With Golden Dome , as with Reagan 's SDI project before it , the law of unintended consequences will make itself felt in potentially terrifying ways . If the traditional concepts of deterrence and " mutually assured destruction " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what might follow . Except , that is , that China and Russia would not meekly do nothing , but would instead seek ways to restore the balance of power . <p> It would not necessarily , as perhaps Reagan once imagined and Trump might now , lead to universal nuclear disarmament . Indeed , back in the 1980s , the Russians regarded SDI as a " provocation " , and the Cold War turned even icier . It took years , aided by the practical difficulties of making SDI a reality , to result in new arms control talks between Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev , and the 1987 intermediate nuclear weapons treaty . <p> Optimistically , maybe Trump 's Golden Dome project will have a happy ending . If peace is the goal , that 's hardly an ignoble ambition -- a golden future . But given the president 's unpredictability and the sheer cost of the programme , the Golden Dome could also make our troubled world even more dangerous . It would be nice to think that our " stable genius " had thought all this stuff through .

In Rerum Novarum , his groundbreaking 1891 papal encyclical , Leo XIII laid out swingeing criticisms of the greed that placed profit before people and allowed extreme divides in wealth to undermine the common good . At the same time , in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in early communist movements a dangerous idolatry of the state and a lack of respect for individual autonomy and rights . <p> Last weekend , before his first mass in St Peter 's Square , Leo XIV explicitly set himself the task of following in his 19th-century predecessor 's footsteps . @@124938859 <h> The virus has been detected in mosquitoes collected in Britain for the first time <p> West Nile Virus has been detected in the UK for the first time , prompting health experts to ramp up surveillance efforts . The UK Health Security Agency ( UKHSA ) and the Animal and Plant Health Agency ( APHA ) have identified fragments of West Nile Virus genetic material in mosquitoes collected in Britain . <p> West Nile Virus is a vector-borne disease from the Flaviviridae family , which also includes the viruses that cause dengue and yellow fever . It is usually found in birds , and typically circulates through bird-biting mosquitoes . <p> ? <p> In rare cases , mosquitoes can transmit the virus to humans or horses . <p> ? <p> The virus is endemic in various regions across the globe , including Europe , Africa , the Middle East , West and Central Asia , and North America , as well as South America , USA and Australia . The geographic range of West Nile Virus has expanded in recent years to more northerly and western regions of mainland @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with West Nile Virus are asymptomatic or present with mild influenza-like symptoms such as fever , headache or myalgia , swollen lymph nodes and a rash . While most mild infections resolve within a few days , a small number of cases ( under 1% ) can cause more severe illness . <p> Dr Meera Chand , UKHSA deputy director for travel health , zoonoses , emerging infections , respiratory and tuberculosis , said : " While this is the first detection of West Nile Virus in mosquitoes in the UK so far , it is not unexpected as the virus is already widespread in Europe . <p> Article continues below <p> " The risk to the general public is currently assessed as very low . Vector research of this kind is designed to give us early warning of potential threats so that we can enhance our disease surveillance and control activities and ensure patients receive appropriate testing . " <p> There have been no cases of locally acquired West Nile Virus detected in humans or horses in the UK to date , although seven travel-associated cases have occurred since @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there is no evidence to suggest ongoing circulation of the virus in birds or mosquitos in the UK . Disease surveillance and control activities are being enhanced in light of the findings . Stay informed on the latest health news by signing up to our newsletter here <p> ? <p> Currently , the main risk of West Nile Virus for UK residents continues to be travel to endemic areas overseas . <p> Dr Arran Folly , Arbovirologist at APHA and lead of the Vector-Borne RADAR project , added : " The detection of West Nile virus in the UK is part of a wider changing landscape , where , in the wake of climate change mosquito-borne diseases are expanding to new areas . @@124942216 <h> The UK must not walk away from its commitment to education <p> Deprioritising support for global education risks trashing the UK 's reputation and devastating consequences for millions of the world 's poorest children . <p> Whilst all eyes were on the EU Summit this week , the UK is also hosting the world 's largest annual gathering of education and skills ministers . <p> The popularity of the event is testimony to the leading role that the UK plays in global education . <p> Overseas students come here to attend our universities , British companies export education services around the world , and UK aid has been central to getting millions of children from the poorest countries into school . <p> However , in preparation for cutting the aid budget to its lowest level in over a quarter of a century , education is on the chopping block . <p> Appearing before the International Development Committee last week , the Minister for International Development , Baroness Chapman , stated that UK support for education will be deprioritised . <p> This will trash our reputation as a long-standing supporter @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will have devastating consequences for millions of the world 's poorest children , who will be denied the opportunity to go to school . <p> Girls like Mapenzi from the Democratic Republic of Congo , who , because of DRC 's brutal civil war , was sent to her grandparents in another part of the country for safety . <p> Unable to afford to send her to school , Mapenzi 's education would have stopped if it were n't for the UK-funded project that allowed Save the Children to step in , pay her school fees , and provide her with the basic supplies she needed to study . <p> This was made possible by the UK-supported Girls Education @@124963771 <h> Get the latest Surrey Live breaking news on WhatsApp <p> A lethal virus has been detected in UK mosquitoes for the first time . The UK Health Security Agency ( UKHSA ) and the Animal and Plant Health Agency ( APHA ) have confirmed the presence of West Nile Virus ( WNV ) genetic material in mosquitoes found in Britain . <p> Following this discovery , Brits are being urged to take action to ' reduce mosquito numbers around our homes ' . This comes after the detection of the virus , which is transmitted to humans by blood-feeding insects , in UK mosquitoes . <p> West Nile Virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family of vector-borne diseases , which also includes viruses responsible for tropical diseases such as dengue fever and yellow fever . The virus is typically found in birds and circulates via bird-biting mosquitoes . In rare instances , mosquitoes can transmit the virus to humans or horses . <h> What are the symptoms ? <p> Most individuals infected with West Nile Virus experience mild flu-like symptoms like fever , headache , muscle aches , swollen lymph @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ maintains that the risk to the public remains ' very low ' , reports the Manchester Evening News . <p> While mild infections usually clear up within a few days , the virus can lead to neurological disease and death in a small number of cases . Nevertheless , approximately 80 per cent of those infected will not exhibit any symptoms . <h> How to avoid mosquitoes <p> Dr Jolyon Medlock , Head of Medical Entomology and Zoonoses Ecology at UKHSA , explained : " Mosquitoes breed in a range of natural wetlands , but can also be common in gardens , breeding in container habitats like water butts and buckets . " <p> UK gardeners have been advised to place lids on water butts and buckets or turn them upside down following the detection of West Nile Virus ( WNV ) . @@124981876 <p> WASHINGTON -- Donald Trump wants to beat China in just about every market -- but he 'd rather take the loss on clean energy . <p> In his second term , the U.S. president has returned more committed than ever to promoting fossil fuels and crushing clean , renewable power sources that do n't burn the planet . <p> Trump 's view is that China has already won the clean energy race , due in part to practices such as forced labor , massive subsidies and intellectual property theft . Trying to compete with Beijing would just make the United States the loser . The president wants the U.S. to focus on energy sources it already dominates , including oil , natural gas and coal . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> That represents a complete break from Trump 's predecessor , Joe Biden , who sought to go toe-to-toe with China in a race for clean energy dominance . Not only that , it contrasts with Trump 's first term , when the White House took an all-you-can-eat-buffet approach to energy and clean power . <p> The new stance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And in Washington , it 's opening up a fundamental divide within Trump 's Republican Party as it works through spending talks . <p> " The second administration is really not about taking half-measures , " said Daniel Simmons , who ran the Energy Department 's energy efficiency and renewable energy office in Trump 's first term . " To all appearances , it is not a battlefield that they care about . " <h> GOP fissures <p> Not all Republicans are ready to let China , Europe and other nations win the clean energy race by default . <p> That intra-GOP division is boiling underneath one of the biggest political controversies in Washington right now : the complicated passage of Trump 's " big , beautiful " tax and spending megabill . <p> Hard-line conservatives are demanding that the bill include a wholesale gutting of hundreds of billions of dollars in Biden-era clean energy tax incentives , which were aimed at juicing U.S. competitors to Chinese and European manufacturers . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> That push threatens to alienate moderate Republicans whose communities stand to gain from factories @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ who had hoped they could win Trump to their side by framing the incentives as the key to edging out China . <p> The message they 've gotten instead : When it comes to winning on clean energy , Trump just is n't interested . <p> Trump 's Energy Department confirmed as much in a statement to POLITICO that focused largely on oil -- an energy source that the U.S. produces more of than any other country . <p> " Thanks to President Trump , America is leading the way in lowering costs by removing red tape and unleashing affordable , abundant , and reliable American energy , " the department said Friday . " As the world 's largest oil producer , the United States welcomes a secure and stable global supply of oil that promotes economic prosperity at home and promotes peace and stability around the world . " <p> The White House referred questions about its clean energy worldview to the Energy Department . <h> Drilling to beat China ? <p> Trump officials have argued that putting any money into green technology boosts China , which dominates @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ solar and wind energy supply chains . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Trump 's zero-sum assessment of the clean energy market has forged an energy strategy even more reliant on fossil fuels than he pursued in his first term . Following this approach would jeopardize a U.S. clean energy manufacturing industry that is just beginning to sprout -- and , green tech advocates say , all but ensure that China will command the global sector . <p> That vision is coming to a head in Congress , where Republicans are working to slash the clean energy incentives created by Biden 's Inflation Reduction Act . While not proposing to erase the tax breaks altogether , GOP lawmakers in the House have floated tight restrictions outlawing Chinese sourcing in the supply chains of energy projects . Those limits would render most of the tax credits unusable for projects that have not yet been built , effectively squelching the nascent U.S. clean manufacturing sector . <p> The changes remain in limbo as part of the broader budget reconciliation bill , the legislative vehicle for green-lighting Republicans ' and Trump 's policy agenda @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . House Republicans are trying to forge a compromise among fiscal conservatives and blocs of GOP lawmakers that want to preserve clean energy credits and raise tax deduction caps for state and local taxes . <p> Trump 's presence looms over the negotiations . He has repeatedly vowed to end Biden 's programs -- the nation 's largest-ever investment in clean energy and fighting climate change -- while labeling them the " green new scam . " Cutting many of those policies , such as consumer credits to purchase electric vehicles , would fund a small portion of his administration 's other priorities , including trillions of dollars in tax breaks . <p> " They do n't see climate change as a problem , " George David Banks , who ran Trump 's first-term climate portfolio , said of the current team 's outlook . He added : " They do n't want to essentially create a jobs program for China . " <p> Overturning the subsidies wouldeliminate a potential U.S. export market for solar modules and batteries that could be worth as much as $50 billion by 2030 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Other countries would fill an $80 billion investment gap left by shuttered U.S. solar facilities , electric vehicle shops and battery gigafactories . <p> Many countries stand to benefit from the U.S. vacating the space , the Johns Hopkins researchers wrote . But governments outside the U.S. would face risks as well : Those that fail to encourage cleantech investments at home may fall even further behind China , which would likely benefit in every industrial category . <p> The researchers also raised the prospect of a transition of intellectual property to China . As U.S. businesses shuttered , they said , foreign companies could purchase their technical knowledge at fire-sale prices . <p> Donald Trump 's barrage of tariffs against nations worldwide would limit some of the advantage countries could gain by selling clean technology to the U.S. , said Tim Sahay , one of the authors of the study . Use of the semicolon ( in lists , or to join two separate clauses into a single sentence ) has almost halved since 2000 and , according to research by language service Babbel , many young Brits never use it at all . <p> Fear of ' using it incorrectly'It 's not that young people are " rejecting " the semicolon outright , said The Telegraph ; " rather , they fear using it incorrectly " . The mark , designed to introduce " a somewhat longer breath " than a comma into a sentence , has been increasingly abandoned by contemporary writers and is now often misunderstood by Gen Z. <p> It 's far from the first punctuation casualty , said The Indian Express . And , in modern times , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ For younger generations , raised on texting and social media , traditional punctuation can sometimes feel " passive-aggressive " or " unnatural " , said The Washington Post . Instead , they punctuate messages with emojis , which act as " tone tags " to convey the sender 's intent . <p> ' The ChatGPT hyphen'The semicolon may be endangered but there is one form of punctuation that seems to be flourishing : the em dash . It is an area of ongoing , and often violent , conflict between Indigenous people and illegal loggers , poachers and fishers , a conflict made worse by traffickers , taking advantage of the lack of state enforcement to use the region 's waterways as a route for smuggling drugs and guns . <p> It is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ places . The ODI Global report found that climate change contributed to at least $11.5bn in losses and damages to livestock and crops in these countries , causing lasting harm to livelihoods and food supplies in agrarian areas with already high poverty rates . <p> Nigeria , Kenya , Uganda and Ethiopia have suffered @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but Somalia has suffered the worst of all . Devastating droughts and subsequent floods have led to $151bn in losses and damages , $75bn of which ODI Global estimates is attributable to climate change . <p> Somalia 's extended droughts have been exacerbated by the climate crisis , researchers have found , contributing to lower rainfall , warmer air temperatures , and higher evapotranspiration -- the combined processes that move water from the Earth 's surface into the atmosphere . <p> These droughts in recent years have caused widespread crop failures and livestock losses , plunging many farmers and herders into poverty . Nearly half of Somalia 's eight-million-strong population has also faced food insecurity . As The Independent has reported , Somalia is facing drought and low crop yields once again ; this time , charities are worried that aid cuts will limit their ability to respond to food shortages . <p> Many of the nations included in the ODI Global study have smaller economies , increasing the impact of climate crisis-related losses . On the Caribbean island of Dominica , such damage has cost nearly a tenth ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) each year on average over the last two decades . <p> Haiti , Kenya and Grenada are among the nations already facing substantial losses , more than two per cent of their GDP per year , thanks to climate change . Extreme weather events such as hurricanes can increase that number substantially , given the damage they can do quickly . <p> This means that poorer nations , some of whom are facing further strain from regional conflicts , are disproportionately taking the brunt of climate-related destruction . <p> These effects will only continue to get worse , warn ODI Global 's researchers , who estimate at least a further $235bn in these countries from climate-related damages if the planet warms by 2C compared to pre-industrial levels . According to climate scientists at Europe 's Copernicus Climate Change Service ( C3S ) , each of the past 10 years ( 2015 -- 2024 ) was one of the 10 warmest years on record . @@125098057 <p> Men generally have bigger feet than women -- and a bigger carbon footprint too , according to new research . <p> A joint UK-French study , at the LSE 's Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment , found that men cause 26% more planet-warming gas emissions than women do , mainly because of the cars they drive and the meat they eat . <p> The researchers analysed French survey data on food consumption and transport patterns -- the two factors that , together , account for 50% of the carbon footprint of French households . They found that , for men , the average annual carbon footprint associated with food and transport was 5.3 tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent ; for women , it was 3.9 . <p> The difference between the sexes is mainly accounted for by men 's higher consumption of red meat and greater use of cars -- both " often associated with male identity " , concluded the study authors in an LSE press release . " Our results suggest that traditional gender norms , particularly those linking masculinity with red-meat consumption and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ carbon footprints , " said study co-author Ondine Berland , a LSE fellow in environmental economics . <h> ' Striking ' gender gap <p> " Research into gender gaps is often plagued by difficult decisions about which factors to control for , " said The Guardian . Men need more calories than women , for example , but " they also eat disproportionately more than women " . Men also tend to drive longer distances when commuting , and they also generally have higher incomes , which are themselves " correlated with higher emissions " . <p> But , even after the study authors controlled for socioeconomic factors such as income , job type , household size and education , the emissions gap between men and women was still a significant 18% . <p> It is " quite striking that the difference in carbon footprint in food and transport use " between French men and women is " around the same as we estimate " globally for high-income people compared to lower-income people , study co-author Marion Leroutier , an assistant professor at Crest-Ensae Paris ? , told the paper @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ study identifies could help explain " the growing climate concern gap between men and women " , said The Independent . It 's possible that men are less inclined to support climate action because there are " higher personal costs " for them in doing so , such as giving up red meat and reducing car use . <p> Alternatively , it could be that women 's lower-carbon lifestyles " might reflect and reinforce deeper values and priorities " : their carbon footprints are smaller because they 're more concerned about the climate . <p> Either way , it 's clear that " public messaging and policy design " on lowering emissions needs " to take social norms and gender roles into account , not just market signals or price incentives " . Strategists wanting to target " high-emission activities like driving and eating meat " need to factor in that this will " disproportionately affect men , especially those who associate consumption with identity or status " . <p> And the rewards of successful messaging could be impressive . If all adult men adopted the average food and transport @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ authors , France 's emissions from food and transport would fall by more than 13 million tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent a year . @@125163024 <h> Your support helps us to tell the story <p> From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech , The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing . We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone , paid for by those who can afford it . <p> You might have a phone charger plugged in next to your bed without ever bothering to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not in use . The same might go for a laptop charger by your desk . <p> But is that risky to do ? And are there hidden costs associated with leaving chargers plugged in all the time ? <h> What 's inside a charger ? <p> Naturally , not all chargers are the same . Depending on the application and power requirement , their internal structure can range from very simple to complex . <p> However , a typical charger takes in the AC ( alternating current ) from the wall plug and converts it to a low-voltage DC ( direct current ) suitable for your device 's battery . <p> To understand the difference between DC and AC , consider the flow of electrons in a wire . In a DC circuit , electrons move in one direction and keep rotating in the circuit . In an AC circuit , electrons do n't circulate and only move back and forth . <p> The reason why we use both types of current goes a long way back , to the time when inventors Thomas Edison and Nicola Tesla battled @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Today , we are still stuck between both . Electricity is traditionally generated in AC form , but modern appliances and batteries require the DC form . This is why almost every electrical appliance comes with an AC -- DC converter . <p> To do the conversion from AC to DC , a typical charger needs several electrical components such as a transformer , a circuit for doing the actual conversion , filtering elements to enhance the quality of output DC voltage , and control circuitry for regulation and protection . <h> Chargers consume power even when not charging <p> " Vampire power " is real . If you leave it plugged in , a charger will continuously draw a small amount of power . Part of this power is used to keep the control and protection circuits running , while the rest is lost as heat . <p> When we look at an individual small charger , the vampire power -- also known as standby power -- is negligible . However , if you add up all the chargers in your home for various devices , over time , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is not exclusive to chargers , either ; other electronic devices such as TVs draw a little bit of standby power , too . <p> To do the conversion from AC to DC , a typical charger needs several electrical components such as a transformer ( Getty Images/iStockphoto ) <p> Depending on how many things you leave plugged in , over the course of the year , it could amount to several kilowatt hours . <p> That said , modern chargers are designed to minimise standby power consumption . These chargers come with smart power management components that keep them in sleep mode until an external device attempts to draw power . <h> There are other risks , too <p> Chargers wear out over time when electricity flows through them , particularly when the electricity grid voltage temporarily rises above its rated value . <p> The electricity grid is a chaotic environment and various voltage rise events happen from time to time . <p> Leaving your chargers exposed to these events will shorten their life . This premature ageing should n't be alarming for modern devices , thanks to their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for cheap , uncertified chargers . These often lack appropriate levels of protection and can be a fire hazard . <h> How should I treat my chargers ? <p> Although modern chargers are generally very safe and should be drawing minimal standby power , consider unplugging them anyway , if convenient . <p> If a charger gets warmer than usual , makes noise , or is damaged in any way , it is time for a replacement . And it definitely should n't be left plugged in . <p> Glen Farivar is a Lecturer in Power Electronics at The University of Melbourne . <p> This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article .

Higher temperatures have been linked to an increased risk of breast , ovarian , uterine , and cervical cancers . <p> Scientists found that climate change in the Middle East and North Africa is making breast , ovarian , uterine , and cervical cancer more common and more deadly . They say the rise in rates is " small but statistically significant " - suggesting a notable increase in cancer risk and fatalities over time . <p> Study first author Dr Wafa Abuelkheir Mataria , of the American University in Cairo , Egypt , said : " As temperatures rise , cancer mortality among women also rises - particularly for ovarian and breast cancers . Although the increases per degree of temperature rise are modest , their cumulative public health impact is substantial . " <p> She said rising temperatures , compromised food and water security , and poor air quality as a result of climate change all increase the burden of disease @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unanticipated weather conditions also disrupt infrastructure , including healthcare systems . <p> When it comes to cancer , the researchers say that can mean people are more exposed to risk factors such as environmental toxins and are less likely to receive a prompt diagnosis and treatment . The team believe the combination of factors could lead to a " major rise " in the incidence of serious cancers , but quantifying it is difficult . <p> The team say those countries are " seriously vulnerable " to climate change and are already seeing " striking " temperature rises . They collected data on the prevalence and mortality of breast cancer , ovarian cancer , cervical cancer , and uterine cancer , and compared this information with changing temperatures between 1998 and 2019 . <p> Co-author Dr Sungsoo Chun , also of the American University in Cairo , said : " Women are physiologically more vulnerable to climate-related health risks , particularly during pregnancy . This is compounded by inequalities that limit access to healthcare . <p> " Marginalised women face a multiplied risk because they are more exposed to environmental @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ services . " <p> The prevalence of the different cancers rose by 173 to 280 cases per 100,000 people for every additional degree Celsius , according to the findings published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health . Ovarian cancer cases rose the most and breast cancer cases the least . <p> Mortality rose by 171 to 332 deaths per 100,000 people for each degree of temperature rise , with the greatest rise in ovarian cancer and the smallest in cervical cancer . When the researchers broke the figures down by country , they found that cancer prevalence and deaths rose in only six countries : Qatar , Bahrain , Jordan , Saudi Arabia , the United Arab Emirates , and Syria . <p> They say that could be due to " particularly extreme " summer temperatures in those countries , or other factors which the model could n't capture . For example , increased heat could be associated with higher levels of carcinogenic air pollution in some places . <p> Dr Chun said : " Temperature rise likely acts through multiple pathways . It increases exposure to known carcinogens , disrupts healthcare delivery , and may even influence biological processes at the cellular level . <p> " Together , these mechanisms could elevate cancer risk over time . " <p> She said higher prevalence could also reflect improvements in cancer screening . Better screening would be expected to result in fewer deaths , as early-stage cancer is easier to treat . <p> But both death rates and prevalence rose , suggesting that the driving factor is exposure to risk factors . @@125205548 <h> Something of ' serious concern ' is happening to a huge area of Earth 's ocean with big consequences <h> The changes could have a profound impact on marine life and our lives as a result <p> New research has exposed a significant and concerning change in our oceans . More than a fifth of the Earth 's ocean has become darker over the past two decades . <p> This process takes place when changes to the ocean 's top layer diminish the depths reached by sunlight . The study identified that a region exceeding 75 million square kilometres -- the habitat for 90% of all marine life -- experienced darkening between 2003 and 2022 . <p> ? <p> Scientists from the University of Plymouth and Plymouth Marine Laboratory have scrutinised NASA satellite imagery and numerical models to determine the yearly fluctuations in the depth sunlight hits the Earth 's oceans , reports the Manchester Evening News . <p> ? <p> They discovered that 21% of the global ocean had seen a darkening effect over the last two decades -- with researchers warning that this could impinge on " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ our ability to fight climate change , and for the general health and wellbeing of the planet " . <p> Dr Thomas Davies , associate professor of marine conservation at the University of Plymouth , explained : " There has been research showing how the surface of the ocean has changed colour over the last 20 years , potentially as a result of changes in plankton communities . " <p> " But our results provide evidence that such changes cause widespread darkening that reduces the amount of ocean available for animals that rely on the sun and the moon for their survival and reproduction . " <p> ? <p> " We also rely on the ocean and its photic zones for the air we breathe , the fish we eat , our ability to fight climate change , and for the general health and wellbeing of the planet . Taking all of that into account , our findings represent genuine cause for concern . " For our free daily briefing on the biggest issues facing the nation , sign up to the Wales Matters newsletter here . <p> Satellite images @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has become darker ( Image : Getty Images ) <p> ? <p> The study also discovered that over 9% of the ocean -- an area comparable in size to the continent of Africa -- has been impacted by a reduction in the sunlight-receiving layer of water , making it 50 metres shallower . Meanwhile , 2.6% has become more than 100 metres shallower . <p> In contrast , the research identified that approximately 10% of the ocean became brighter . While the exact effects of these alterations remain unclear , they have the potential to hugely affect marine life across the globe , experts warn . <p> Professor Tim Smyth , head of science for marine biogeochemistry and observations at Plymouth Marine Laboratory , remarked : " The ocean is far more dynamic than it is often given credit for . <p> ? <p> " For example , we know the light levels within the water column vary massively over any 24-hour period , and animals whose behaviour is directly influenced by light are far more sensitive to its processes and change . <p> " If the photic zone is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , animals that need light will be forced closer to the surface where they will have to compete for food and the other resources they need . <p> " That could bring about fundamental changes in the entire marine ecosystem . " <p> Ms Valverde said she expected participants to make commitments totalling $100 billion ( around ? 75bn ) in new funding to address the crisis facing the oceans . <p> French UN ambassador Jerome Bonnafont said his country 's priorities for the conference included obtaining 60 ratifications of the treaty to protect biodiversity in the high seas , which was adopted in March 2023 , so that it comes into force . <p> The treaty 's mission is to ensure sustainable fishing , mobilise support to protect and conserve at least 30 per cent of the oceans ' waters , fight plastic pollution , " accelerate decarbonisation " of maritime transport and mobilise financing . <p> Conference participants are expected to adopt a declaration that says action is not advancing fast enough to address the impact of " the triple planetary crisis of climate change , biodiversity loss and pollution . <p> " We underscore the central role of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , ensuring global food security and supporting billions of lives , " the final draft says . <p> The United States said last week that it would consider selling leases to extract minerals from the seabed off the South Pacific island of American Samoa . <p> This could be the first step in a wider industry push to allow deep-sea mining , which environmentalists say could do irreparable harm to marine ecosystems .

There are tough decisions ahead on expenditure : satellites , fighter jets and state-of-the-art cyber-weapons do not come cheap . But we need them all . <p> As a matter of urgency , the new Europe will also have to reassess the balance between regulation and economic dynamism . Trump 's tariffs are scaring off investors . But , to attract those trillions of dollars , Europe must convince a sceptical world that its love of rules offers stability rather than intolerable bureaucracy and red tape . <p> If this continent -- including the UK -- is truly to compete with the US and China , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ so miserably to nurture tech start-ups . Europe 's fatal flaw is self-congratulation , especially in contrast to the supposed vulgarities and Darwinian social policies of America . But our energies should be focused on more practical issues now . We need the vigour of Sparta , as much as the wisdom of Athens . <p> Why , for instance , is it so hard to imagine a European version of Meta being founded in London , Berlin or Madrid ? And , if the US really is off the pitch when it comes to strategic defence , how quickly can Europe muster a regional barrier against further Russian aggression ? <p> How soon before European forces could pull off -- for example -- an operation as bold as SEAL Team Six 's assassination of Osama bin Laden in 2011 ? There will be moments when dormant Nato springs back into life and America joins in . But we can no longer depend upon that . Will the new Europe be capable of fighting a kinetic war unaided by the US ; or a decisive response to the next iteration @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that are rising across the continent ? <p> These are uncomfortable questions , and they are meant to be . If the Old World is to become the New New World , it must practise the most searching self-scrutiny . <p> Winston Churchill was right in 1949 , as the Council of Europe was being developed , to observe that purpose and ethos count for more than the nuts and bolts of structures . " I hope we should not put our trust in formulae or in machinery , " he said , adding that it was " the growth and gathering of the united sentiment of Europeanism " that mattered . <p> So : what form will the new Europe take ? An EU+ ? An EPC with legal and military power ? An evolving but informal coalition of the willing across sectors ? It is too early to say . <p> What is certain is that the work ahead will be extremely difficult and involve a doctrinal and practical agility that has not been the EU 's strongest suit . But the alternative is a supine slide to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the future . <p> As Gramsci wrote in 1930 : " The old world is dying , and the new world struggles to be born : now is the time of monsters " . @@125265491 <p> Retailers are facing a particularly challenging moment in time . Economic pressures , rising sustainability concerns , and consumers ' growing exhaustion with screens are all forcing retailers to adopt new strategies to deliver more effortless customer experiences , improve sustainability , and support interactions that feel more authentic and consistent . Forward-thinking brands are turning these challenges into opportunities by embracing cutting-edge technologies , both for customer-facing and behind-the-scenes use cases . <h> Autonomous AI agents <p> The most recent Futurescape trend report from creative consultancy frog , part of Capgemini Invent , anticipates a near future of : " effortless purchasing where personal AI agents anticipate needs , handle weekly shopping and assist with major buying decisions . " The report also predicts that : " the series of screens and interfaces that we interact with daily will fade as technology integrates so seamlessly with life . " <p> One way to make shopping experiences easier and less screen-focused is through the use of autonomous AI agents . OpenAI 's recently released Operator AI agent promises to help retailers deliver this kind of experience . This AI @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where it can scroll , click , enter data , and consume information to accomplish tasks requested by the user . Operator is still in its early stages , and OpenAI is working with retailers and retail delivery services -- including Etsy , eBay , and Instacart -- to test and refine the technology . <p> Operator and other AI agents have the potential to liberate consumers from clicking through websites to find products and complete transactions . They can also provide retailers with data to help them optimize their operations and improve their personalization . <p> Agentic AI is n't the only path away from screens as the primary interface for customer interactions , though . For example , Continental 's zero UI driver authentication feature uses biometrics to validate a driver 's identity , unlock and start vehicles , and enable in-car payments . Because the technology is embedded in the vehicle , using it feels as natural as walking up to the car , getting in , and driving . Retailers could use similar technologies to allow seamless in-store shopping experiences . <h> Scaling sustainability <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for consumers , and close to 60% say they 've become more concerned about climate change during the past two years . New technology offers both short- and long-term pathways to more circular production and consumption . For example , digital product passports that indicate product inputs , care , and recycling instructions can : " promote transparency to consumers and other stakeholders , " per a recent Deloitte report . <p> Tracking and presenting product passport data from complex supply chains can be a huge and expensive undertaking . AI can help by making those supply chains more transparent " through the use of machine learning , big data analytics , and blockchain integration . " Some manufacturers and brands are already using AI for supply chain visibility . Longer-term AI use cases for circularity include materials research and design , to identify more sustainable inputs faster . <p> Alongside AI , biodesign harnesses natural processes and materials to create products that require fewer unsustainable inputs and can be recycled or repurposed more easily than traditional alternatives . For example , noted circular design innovator William McDonough recently collaborated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ create a system of modular , configurable furniture that users can adapt to their needs and settings . Following McDonough 's ' Cradle to Cradle ' principles of safe , sustainable inputs and a practical plan for recycling or re-use , the Twist collection is made from plant-based materials , and each piece has a digital product passport with recycling instructions . Items from the collection can be 3D printed on demand close to the end user , reducing material waste and transportation-related emissions . <h> Rethinking retail <p> Although the tools we 've discussed here are based on advanced technology , they also have the potential to humanize customer experiences that too often feel fragmented or inauthentic . Eighty-eight percent of consumers say authenticity is a central consideration in their decision to support a brand . So , as retailers and consumer brands expand their use of AI and automation to drive more efficiency and personalization , they can reallocate some of the resources they free up to craft more consistent , authentic messaging . <p> AI agents can help deliver these more authentic experiences . Because they know @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the buying cycle , these agents have the potential to act as a reliable guide , assistant , and confidante as consumers research and make buying decisions . Other zero-UI experiences that allow for seamless shopping and buying decisions in-store can also free consumers to engage more with store staff or with their shopping companions , creating a more social experience that meets the need for greater connection . <p> All these innovations present opportunities for retailers to build stronger connections with consumers by reimagining how shopping and purchasing can work . At a time when many consumers are feeling multiple stressors , the retail brands that make shopping easier , more sustainable , and more natural and authentic will be in the best position to weather today 's challenges and those of tomorrow as well .

@@125283125 <p> Across social media , you 'll often see posts citing the World Happiness Report -- headlines like " Finland ranked the happiest country in the world " or " Why does country X have such a low happiness index ? " What many do n't realise is that the man behind this report is a Cambridge alumnus . <p> Sitting across from us in the Union 's Members ' Room is Baron Richard Layard . Matriculating in 1954 at King 's College , Layard joined Cambridge to read history after being in the army . Wearing a bright orange hat and a circular pin on his jacket reading ' Action for Happiness ' , he returns to Cambridge for a talk at the Union . <p> Happiness has long been a central concern . Yet , few may be familiar with the field of happiness economics , an area that Layard has helped pioneer since the 1970s . Entering the field of economics in his 30s , Layard went on to co-develop the influential Layard-Nickell model of unemployment in the 1980s , still widely used by economists and policymakers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : was Layard a happy student at Cambridge in the 50s ? " <p> We had to know : was Layard a happy student at Cambridge in the 50s ? Layard says yes , but the only time he " felt slightly depressed " was the beginning . He recalled the difficult transition from the " real life " he had in the army . Despite the initial stress , he spoke warmly of his experience here . Revealing the competitive atmosphere that shapes the university today , Layard expressed surprise . In his day , " students were n't competing with each other and most aspired to public service roles such as teaching , medicine , or the civil service " . An answer that certainly surprised us . <p> For Layard , he views academia as " a more disciplined way of thinking about policies " . His whole life , he has tended to think about " the big issues " and the " one particular policy " he wants to push . For him , that policy is the policy of happiness . <p> Layad holds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Aristotelian virtue ethics . He views the aim of all human activity to be " maximising happiness " , but " you 're not going to be doing a calculus every moment of the day " . Instead , " you 've got to operate by some rule of thumb " in general . He differentiates between these two modes of thinking , referencing the book Thinking Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman . <p> Layard believes that these principles should guide both private action and public policy . Since the 1970s , he has advocated for policies that maximise social welfare based on how much happiness they can generate across societies . <p> " Everybody has an interest in the maintenance of peace everywhere " <p> Crucially , Layard views happiness to have global relevance . Emphasising the need for " international collaboration " for issues such as climate change , he acknowledged its obstacles . However , he underscored the imperative for countries to recognise their common interests . Above all , he highlighted the universal stake we all have in peace : " everybody has an interest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the World Happiness Report in 2012 , Layard offered a global perspective on life satisfaction . His key takeaway is that public spending should reflect what people truly value . In recent years , Layard has focused on mental health and wellbeing , arguing that these should be regarded as central to happiness on individual , national , and international levels . As a member of the House of Lords , he even helped to introduce mindfulness courses to Parliament . <p> As our interview came to a close , we asked the man who has spent decades researching happiness the ultimate question : what makes him happy ? His answer was surprisingly simple : " my wife , my work , doing something useful , and tennis " . <p> Happiness can serve as both a national and international policy goal . However , Layard 's answer reveals a deeper truth -- happiness in the everyday sense is found in the simple things like the people we love , the work we value , and the simple moments of joy we encounter . For its 100th episode , The Infinite Monkey Cage brought together science experts and enthusiastic amateurs to discuss some of the most strange and surprising discoveries -- from Saturn 's secrets to Neanderthal genes in our DNA ... <h> 1 . The elusive Higgs boson particle <h> Also known as " the God particle " , the Higgs boson was discovered in 2012 by scientists working in the Large Hadron Collider at CERN . <p> The Higgs had long been thought to exist by physicists , but no one had been able to prove it before . This mysterious subatomic particle is what gives other particles their mass . <p> The significance of the discovery for our everyday lives is yet to be seen . But as astrophysicist Neil De Grasse Tyson says , when quantum physics was discovered people wondered what use it would be , yet today , decades later , it 's " the foundation of the entire information technology revolution " . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Einstein first predicted the existence of gravitational waves -- ripples in the structure of space and time -- in his Theory of General Relativity , over 100 years ago . <p> At the time , Einstein believed it would never be possible to directly observe gravitational waves . However , in the last ten years scientists have developed technology sophisticated enough to detect these tiny oscillations . <p> It 's as if we only had sight before , but now we can actually hear . <p> Prof Fay Dowker <p> Gravitational waves are produced by massive events , such as the collision of two huge black holes , which create ripples that travel billions of light years outwards across the galaxy to reach us . <p> Physicist Prof Fay Dowker says the discovery heralds " a new era of gravitational wave astronomy " , describing it as like gaining a new sense : " It 's as if we only had sight before , but now we can actually hear . " <h> 4 . Our ancestors interbred with other species <h> The Neanderthals may have been extinct for thousands @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ enabled geneticists to map the Neanderthal genome using DNA extracted from ancient bones . This led to a startling discovery : our ancestors interbred with other species after they migrated out of Africa . <p> So in the UK , most of us have a small percentage of Neanderthal genes in our DNA , and scientists have found traces of the Denisovans and other ancient hominid species too . <p> In short , as Prof Alice Roberts , an anatomist and anthropologist from the University of Birmingham explains , " We just really were n't clear about the level of shenanigans that went on in human evolution , and now we are . " <h> 5 . Scientists have created a " mini-brain " using Neanderthal DNA <h> Using advanced genetic editing techniques , scientists have been able to replace or delete parts of human DNA with Neanderthal genes and use stem cells to grow an " organoid " -- a pea-sized group of cells that acts like a mini-brain , carrying electrical signals . <p> As Sue Black , an anatomist and forensic scientist from the University of Lancaster @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ link the electrical signals up to a robot , and " see if they can actually get Neanderthal genes orchestrating movement in another object . " <p> Scientists have been able to replace or delete parts of human DNA with Neanderthal genes . <h> 6 . Young people are now much less likely to drink , take drugs or get pregnant <h> Statistics have revealed fascinating things about how health and lifestyles have changed over the last decade , especially among young people . <p> Fewer people aged 18-24 now take drugs and less than half have an alcoholic drink each week . Smoking has decreased by a quarter , too . But the most remarkable change has been in teenage pregnancy rates , which have halved since 2009 -- from 1 in 30 to less than 1 in 60. <h> 7 . @@125329772 <h> ' Empathy is a kind of strength ' : Jacinda Ardern on kind leadership , public rage and life in Trump 's America <p> Young , progressive and relatable , the former prime minister of New Zealand tried to do politics differently . But six years into power , she dramatically resigned . In an exclusive interview with the Guardian 's editor-in-chief , she explains why <p> In 2022 , a few months before she quit as prime minister of New Zealand , Jacinda Ardern was standing at the sink in the toilets in Auckland airport , washing her hands , when a woman came up to her and leaned in . She was so close that Ardern could feel the heat from her skin . " I just wanted to say thank you , " the woman said . " Thanks for ruining the country . " She turned and left , leaving Ardern " standing there as if I were a high-schooler who 'd just been razed " . <p> The incident was deeply shocking . Ardern had been re-elected in a historic landslide two years before @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the kind of leader who was n't sealed off from the rest of the population . But this , says Ardern , " felt like something new . It was the tenor of the woman 's voice , the way she 'd stood so close , the way her seething , nonspecific rage felt not only unpredictable but incongruous to the situation ... What was happening ? " <p> Jacinda Ardern photographed in New York last month . Photograph : Benedict Evans/The Guardian <p> The incident came at a pivotal moment : Ardern sensed that the tide was turning against her and she was grappling with whether to go . " Something had been loosened worldwide , " she says , with rage everywhere , public servants being followed and attacked , as if they were " somehow distinct from being human " . We all recognise this rage , but Ardern was at the centre of it , representing progressive politics , tough Covid measures , empathy , emotion , anti-racism , femaleness ; a symbol of a different time , more rational , kinder , when rules still @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Angela Merkel , Theresa May , Sanna Marin , Mia Mottley , Mette Frederiksen , Tsai Ing-wen . <p> For all these reasons , Ardern is now missed by progressives , at home and abroad . At her height she had blazed a global trail , modelling a different way of doing politics -- wearing a headscarf and embracing weeping bereaved families after the Christchurch mosque massacre , then reforming gun laws in 10 days ; taking decisive action on Covid that meant New Zealanders were able to party again while the rest of the world could barely go out ; leaving celebrities from Elton John to Stephen Colbert starry-eyed with her poise and wit and humanity . It was Jacinda-mania , and everybody wanted a prime minister like her : young ( elected at just 37 ) and a woman , she offered a different vision of national identity for New Zealand -- straightforward , compassionate , diverse , globally desirable -- and a different way to lead a country -- youthful , human , decent . She had a hunky feminist boyfriend and was pregnant when she became @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ back " . <p> And then , out of the blue , after six years in office , in January 2023 , she dramatically announced her resignation .
